agency: Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services (DPHHS), Human and Community Services Division (HCSD)
agency_short: Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services (DPHHS)
admin_note: Montana is a STATE-ADMINISTERED SNAP program — DPHHS's Human and Community Services Division (HCSD) administers directly through local Offices of Public Assistance (OPA), with no county-level policy variation, structurally similar to this roster's Nebraska, Connecticut, North Carolina, Ohio, New Jersey, Tennessee, Indiana, Missouri, Maryland, Colorado, South Carolina, Alabama, Louisiana, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Utah, Iowa, Arkansas, Mississippi, Kansas, New Mexico, New Hampshire, Idaho, West Virginia, Hawaii, and Maine packs. GENUINE STRUCTURAL FLAGSHIP FINDING (a correction of a widely-repeated secondary-source oversimplification): several secondary sources (e.g. Propel's own Montana guide) state flatly that "Montana won't disqualify you [from SNAP] because of a drug felony." This pack fetched Montana DPHHS's own current SNAP manual directly (SNAP 304-1, SNAP 001, SNAP 602-4, all effective/current as of the 07/01/2026 Table of Contents) and found the actual rule is a MODIFIED ban, not a full opt-out: an individual convicted after 08/22/96 of a federal or state felony for possession, use, or distribution of illegal drugs is disqualified ONLY IF they are also "not complying with conditions of supervision" (e.g., probation/parole terms, which commonly include treatment-program participation) — an individual who IS complying with supervision conditions is not disqualified on this basis. This pack treats the secondary-source "won't disqualify you" framing as an overclaim that omits the supervision-compliance condition, and reads Montana's actual rule as retaining a real, live disqualification pathway for noncompliant drug felons rather than a genuine full opt-out like this roster's New Hampshire or Maine packs found; see criminal-justice-disqualifications supplement. SECOND FLAGSHIP FINDING: Montana's own DPHHS SNAP 400 (Resources Overview, effective 10/01/2024, current per the 07/01/2026 TOC) states the non-categorically-eligible resource limit is $3,000 for a household with no elderly/disabled member — several secondary sources this pack found instead cite $2,750, a stale figure from an earlier COLA cycle (the federal general SNAP resource limit rose from $2,750 to $3,000 effective the FFY2025 cycle). This pack flags the $2,750 figure as OUTDATED and confirms $3,000/$4,500 (elderly/disabled) as Montana's own currently-published figures; see income-and-resources supplement. THIRD FINDING: Montana operates a genuine Broad-Based-style Expanded Categorical Eligibility (ECE) track at 200% FPG gross income with no resource test, alongside a narrower Traditional Categorical Eligibility (CE, TANF/Tribal TANF/SSI recipients) track and a residual non-CE/non-ECE track that does face the $3,000/$4,500 resource limits and the underlying 130%/100% FPG income tests — a three-track structure this pack reads precisely rather than compressing into a flat "no asset test" claim, matching the same structural caution this roster's New Hampshire pack applied; see income-and-resources supplement. FOURTH FINDING: Montana currently has NO approved ABAWD geographic waivers anywhere in the state, confirmed directly and unambiguously by DPHHS's own SNAP 802-1 ("As of 11/01/2025, there are no areas within Montana with approved ABAWD geographic waivers") — a cleaner, more directly-confirmed finding than several other states in this roster where waiver absence had to be inferred from a waiver index's lack of a current entry. Confirm current operative practice with the applicant's own local Office of Public Assistance, the same caution this roster already carries for its other built states.
system: DPHHS's Human and Community Services Division (HCSD) processes SNAP centrally through local Offices of Public Assistance (OPA, no county offices with independent policy authority); applicants apply online through apply.mt.gov, by calling the Public Assistance Helpline (1-888-706-1535, which can mail a paper application), by emailing a request for a PDF application to hhssspapplicationcustomersupport@mt.gov, by mail, or in person at a local OPA. A phone interview is required to complete the application. SNAP benefits are issued on the Montana Access Card (Montana's state-branded EBT card). Households in which all members are elderly (60+) or disabled with no earned income are certified for 24 months; all other households are certified for 12 months (Simplified Reporting) or, for change-reporting households, up to 24 months with at least one contact required every 12 months — a more conventional certification structure than this roster's New Hampshire pack (6-month standard) or Maine pack.

verification.method: dphhs.mt.gov served every page and PDF this pack needed with a clean, direct HTTP 200 response to a standard browser User-Agent — NO WAF/bot-detection barrier of the kind this roster's New Hampshire and several other packs encountered. This pack located Montana's SNAP manual via its actual current path (dphhs.mt.gov/hcsd/Manuals/SNAPmanual — a case- and path-sensitive URL that differs from an initially-guessed dphhs.mt.gov/HCSD/snapmanual, which 404's) and fetched the current Table of Contents (SNAPTOC7.2026.pdf, dated 07.01.26) to confirm exactly which section numbers and effective dates are currently operative before fetching each individual section PDF directly. All section PDFs this pack fetched (SNAP001, SNAP304-1, SNAP400, SNAP402-1, SNAP403-1, SNAP602-2, SNAP602-3, SNAP602-4, SNAP801-1, SNAP802-1, SNAP1502-1, SNAP0-3, SNAP103-1, SNAP705-1) opened cleanly with pdftotext -layout with no corruption; the one URL-guess miss (SNAP801-1.pdf, which does not exist — the real file is SNAP801.1.pdf) was caught immediately via a file-type check (the failed fetch returned an HTML 404 page, not a PDF) and corrected on retry.
verification.gates: No access barrier of any kind was found at dphhs.mt.gov — every direct curl attempt with a standard browser User-Agent returned a clean HTTP 200, and no Wayback Machine or reader-proxy fallback was needed. The Montana Legislature's mca.legmt.gov site required following two chained 301 redirects (leg.mt.gov -> archive.legmt.gov -> mca.legmt.gov) to reach the current Food Stamp Program statute index (Title 53, Chapter 2, Part 9), which this pack followed successfully; no drug-felony-specific state statute was found there (only 53-2-901 rulemaking authority, 53-2-902 definitions, 53-2-903 E&T, 53-2-904 income/resource exclusions for FAIM participants), consistent with Montana's drug-felony disqualification being implemented through DPHHS administrative rule/policy manual rather than a standalone opt-out statute. fns.usda.gov's Restaurant Meals Program page timed out on direct WebFetch (60s); this pack fell back to WebSearch corroboration for the 9-state RMP list and flags this explicitly as a WebSearch-only source in freshness.json rather than silently treating it as independently fetched.
